summary: The Lottery tax calculator turns the lump sum payout percentage, the lump sum payout and more into annuity payout. That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Lottery tax calculator work?
sections.html:
The Lottery tax calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports annuity payout in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the tax treatment and the federal filing status); then you type in the lump sum payout percentage, the lump sum payout, the tax rate II. and the annuity term.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Lottery tax calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Annuity payout=lump sum payout ÷ lump sum payout percentage
Payout difference=(annuity payout, annuity term, rate of return, annual growth rate, state tax rate, federal filing status, tax treatment, tax rate II., tax rate I., lump sum payout)
Federal lump sum tax 1=((annuity payout, annuity term, rate of return, annual growth rate, state tax rate, federal filing status, tax treatment, tax rate II., tax rate I., lump sum payout))
Federal annuity tax 1=((annuity payout, annuity term, rate of return, annual growth rate, state tax rate, federal filing status, tax treatment, tax rate II., tax rate I., lump sum payout))
Federal difference tax 1=((annuity payout, annuity term, rate of return, annual growth rate, state tax rate, federal filing status, tax treatment, tax rate II., tax rate I., lump sum payout))
State lump sum tax 2=((annuity payout, annuity term, rate of return, annual growth rate, state tax rate, federal filing status, tax treatment, tax rate II., tax rate I., lump sum payout))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Lottery tax calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the lump sum payout percentage, the lump sum payout and the tax rate II. — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Lottery tax calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns annuity payout, derived from the lump sum payout percentage, the lump sum payout and the tax rate II.. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Lottery tax calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the lump sum payout percentage, the lump sum payout, the tax rate II. and the annuity term, which is 28 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter annuity payout in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Annuity payout opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Lump sum payout = 52000000. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Lottery tax calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
